name: Pittsburgh International Airport
before:
Pittsburgh's airport, about 17 miles west of downtown, serving the wider region and adjacent parts of West Virginia and Ohio.

Its history explains why it feels oversized. A one billion dollar rebuild completed in 1992 was designed largely to US Airways' specification so the airport could become one of their major hubs. The result was called the airport of the future by The New York Times and pioneered modern airport design, with an X-shaped layout to cut walking distance between gates, an underground tram between concourses and a large retail offer, all unusual at the time. Traffic peaked around 20 million passengers in the late 1990s, and US Airways alone ran over 500 daily flights with 12,000 staff here in 2001 before the airline became unstable.

Today it offers flights across North America, the Caribbean and Europe.

At 10,000 acres it is the largest civil airport by land area in Pennsylvania, with four runways, and it hosts a sizeable United States Air Force base.
after:
Pittsburgh's airport, about 17 miles west of downtown, serving the wider region. It handled about 9.8 million passengers in 2025.

The airport was rebuilt in 1992 as a connecting hub for US Airways, and The New York Times called it the airport of the future. An underground train linked the landside terminal to an X-shaped airside terminal, built to keep walks between gates short. Traffic peaked at about 20 million passengers in the 1990s. After two bankruptcies, in 2002 and 2004, US Airways gave up the hub.

A new $1.7 billion landside terminal, built for people starting or ending their trips in Pittsburgh, opened on 18 November 2025. Passengers now walk from security across a bridge to the airside gates, and the underground train has been retired.

Today it offers flights across North America, the Caribbean and Europe. It has four runways and hosts a US Air Force base.

claims.claim: adjacent parts of West Virginia and Ohio
claims.wasBefore: and adjacent parts of West Virginia and Ohio
claims.why: Only Wikipedia says so. Three operator pages (air service, cargo and real estate) describe the Pittsburgh region, western Pennsylvania and a two-hour drive time, but not these states.

claims.claim: its history explains why it feels oversized
claims.wasBefore: Its history explains why it feels oversized.
claims.why: Out of date. The new landside terminal of November 2025 was built to right-size the airport (Cranky Flier: 'right-sized for its hub-less reality'); the airside terminal lost a side at the same time. Replaced by what the new terminal is for.

claims.claim: a one billion dollar rebuild
claims.wasBefore: A one billion dollar rebuild completed in 1992
claims.why: The date and the US Airways hub are kept with two sources. The one billion dollar cost rests on Wikipedia alone; Simple Flying repeats it in Wikipedia's own words, so it does not count.

claims.claim: pioneered modern airport design; all unusual at the time
claims.why: Wikipedia's claim; Pittsburgh Magazine says only that it 'served as a model for other airports around the world'. The features themselves are kept, with two sources each.

claims.claim: an underground tram between concourses
claims.why: Wrong and out of date: the train ran between the landside and airside terminals, not between concourses, and it was retired in November 2025. Corrected above.

claims.claim: a large retail offer, all unusual at the time
claims.wasBefore: a large retail offer, all unusual at the time
